title: Nintendo & Capcom Platforming
blurb: The console's foundational run of first-party classics, joined by Capcom's licensed Mega Man and Ninja Gaiden series at their peak.
games: The pack-in that sold the console worldwide, though Europe waited nearly two years after Japan's 1985 launch to get its own copy.
The West's sequel is actually a reskin of the unrelated Japanese game Doki Doki Panic — the real, much harder Japanese Super Mario Bros. 2 never left the Famicom Disk System.
A genre-defining leap in scope and ambition, though Europe had to wait a full three years after Japan's 1988 original release.
Widely considered the series' high point, with a soundtrack still remixed decades later — Europe got it two and a half years after Japan.
Introduces the slide move and rival character Proto Man, released the same year across all three regions.
Adds the charged Mega Buster shot that became a series staple, arriving in Europe a full two years after its Japanese debut.
An unusually tight worldwide release window for the era brought Kirby's first console outing to Japan, North America, and Europe all in the same year.
A Wonder Boy spin-off turned its own franchise, though this one had a genuinely enormous gap — Europe didn't see it until six years after Japan's 1986 original.
Renamed Shadow Warriors in Europe, since 'ninja' branding was considered a harder sell there — famous for its cinematic story cutscenes, unusual for the era.
The Japanese original's Nazi imagery — swastikas, Hitler as the final boss — was censored worldwide for the West: the faction became the fictional 'Badds' and the boss was renamed 'Master-D.'

title: Action-Adventure & Metroidvania
blurb: Zelda, Metroid, and Castlevania all began here, alongside two Sunsoft and Taito cult favorites that took years longer to reach the West.
games: An unusually fast worldwide turnaround for 1987 brought Zelda's open-world debut to all three major regions within about a year of Japan's original release.
Zelda II: The Adventure of Link
A side-scrolling detour from the original's top-down template — Europe actually got it about two months before North America, a reversal of the usual rollout order.
Samus Aran's debut, and one of the first games built explicitly around a mid-game genre-twisting reveal.
Released in Japan as Akumajō Dracula — the whip-cracking vampire hunter format that would define the series for decades.
An open-world, RPG-inflected detour from the original's linear structure, not fully embraced by fans until years later — Europe waited over two years past Japan's release.
The Japanese cartridge, released as Akumajō Densetsu, included an extra VRC6 sound chip for richer audio that Western carts couldn't reproduce.
Released in Japan as Chō Wakusei Senki MetaFight, blending top-down tank exploration with side-scrolling on-foot sections — Europe waited three years for it.
An action-RPG built on Nihon Falcom's Dragon Slayer/Xanadu source material, though Hudson Soft alone developed this specific NES port.
A late-era action-platformer letting you swap between four characters mid-level, now one of the most expensive NES carts on the collector market.

title: Role-Playing Adventures
blurb: Square and Enix's earliest Western RPG exports anchor this chapter — several of which, strikingly, never made it to Europe on NES at all.
games: The series' NES debut in North America — it never received any European NES release; the first PAL players could see it was a 2003 PlayStation compilation.
Enix's foundational console RPG, developed by Chunsoft and released three years after Japan's 1986 Dragon Quest original — never released in Europe on NES.
A prequel with a class-change system years ahead of its time, held back four years from its Japanese release and, like its predecessor, never reached Europe.
Introduces AI-driven party tactics and a multi-chapter structure — released in North America the same year as Japan, but never in Europe.
An action-RPG released in Japan as God Slayer: Haruka Tenkū no Sonata, blending Zelda-style combat with a full magic and armor system — never released in Europe.
An unusual Nintendo-published action-RPG built exclusively for the West — it never released in Japan at all, though it did eventually reach Europe.
A licensed tie-in to the Ron Howard fantasy film that turned out to be a genuinely well-regarded action-RPG in its own right — Europe's release didn't arrive until 1993, four years later.
Released in Japan as Arabian Dream Scheherazade, mixing overhead action with turn-based combat sequences — no European release has been found for it.

title: Run-and-Gun & Shooters
blurb: Konami's Contra duology anchors a chapter full of Compile and Capcom shoot-em-ups, several of which stayed North America-only.
games: Renamed Probotector in Europe, with the human soldiers redesigned as robots to sidestep Germany's strict violence-content rules — a redesign the series repeated for years.
Released in Japan as Super Contra, following Contra's own robot-reskin treatment in Europe under the title Probotector II: Return of the Evil Forces.
Released in Japan as Salamander, with Europe's box combining both names as Life Force: Salamander — a genuine three-way title split across regions.
A horizontal shoot-em-up landmark that introduced the power-up bar system still used across the genre today.
A colorful vertical shooter from the Zanac team with a shop system between stages — no European release has been found for it.
An unusually difficult, adaptive-AI vertical shooter that adjusts enemy patterns to the player's own performance — confirmed never released in the PAL region.
A vertical WWII shoot-em-up sequel to 1942, ported faithfully from the arcade original — no European NES release has been found.
A top-down run-and-gun about rescuing POWs by jeep — Europe only ever got home-computer ports of this one, never an NES cartridge.

title: Beat-em-ups, Wrestling & Fighting
blurb: Technōs Japan's brawlers anchor this chapter, alongside boxing's most famous NES cartridge and a wrestling game developed, unusually, by Rare.
games: A home conversion of the arcade beat-em-up that helped define the genre, published in Europe by Nintendo directly.
A from-the-ground-up NES redesign rather than a straight arcade port, released the same year in North America and Europe.
An RPG-inflected brawler letting you shop for stat upgrades mid-adventure — released in Europe under the different title Street Gangs.
Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles II: The Arcade Game
Renamed Teenage Mutant Hero Turtles II in Europe, the same 'Ninja→Hero' swap the whole franchise carried there over UK broadcast-violence concerns.
Released simultaneously worldwide with Tyson's likeness intact — after his boxing license lapsed in 1990, later production runs everywhere were rebranded to a fictional 'Mr. Dream.'
A top-down run-and-gun adapted from SNK's arcade original by a separate porting studio — Europe's release lagged nearly three years behind Japan's.
A licensed wrestling game developed, notably, by Rare rather than LJN, who only published it.
An arcade beat-em-up conversion published in Japan, unusually, by Namco rather than developer Data East — Europe's release followed about a year later, keeping the same title.

title: Puzzle & Party
blurb: Tetris's NES history is inseparable from a landmark licensing lawsuit; HAL Laboratory's Lolo puzzlers round out a quieter, cerebral chapter.
games: Nintendo's own NES cartridge — a separate release from the earlier Bullet-Proof Software Famicom disk — became NES-exclusive worldwide after Nintendo won a landmark 1989 lawsuit forcing rival publisher Tengen's version off shelves.
A falling-block puzzler pairing Mario with a bottle of pills and two colored viruses, released in Europe about a year after Japan and North America.
A block-pushing puzzle-adventure built from HAL's earlier Japan-only Eggerland series — Europe's release trailed North America's by about two years.
A direct sequel deepening the original's room-by-room puzzle logic, released in Europe the year after its North American debut.
Released very late in the console's commercial life, alongside Japan's AV Famicom relaunch, and developed jointly with Intelligent Systems.
A faithful home conversion of Taito's cooperative arcade classic, arriving in Europe three years after its original Japanese release.
An ice-themed puzzle-platformer actually built by Nanao rather than publisher Irem, released the same year in North America and Europe.
A falling-block puzzler about catching Mario's stacked enemies in two columns — the debut release from Game Freak, years before they'd create Pokémon.

title: Sports & Racing
blurb: Rare's off-road racer and Tecmo's football sim sit alongside two American-sports titles that Europe's smaller, later NES library simply skipped.
games: An early physics-driven motocross racer with a built-in track editor, one of the console's first true system-sellers.
A top-down racer with genuine weapon and item pickups, released day-and-date in North America and Europe — but, unusually, never in Japan at all.
An arcade ice hockey conversion known for its genuinely brutal fight-mode minigame, released in Europe two years after its North American debut.
A minimalist, tactical hockey sim developed by Pax Softnica on Nintendo's behalf, released the same year across Japan, North America, and Europe.
Released in Japan as Highway Star, this pseudo-3D racer even supported the era's red-and-blue 3D glasses as an optional feature.
An arcade-style soccer game from the River City Ransom team, with the same exaggerated special-move combat sensibility applied to free kicks.
A sequel to the arcade button-mashing classic built directly for home consoles — no European NES release has been found for it.
A genuine license coup pairing real NFL teams and players with deep season-management systems — American football never found a European NES audience, so it stayed North America-only.
An early example of a create-a-team sports RPG hybrid, another American-sport title with no European NES release.

title: Simulation & Strategy
blurb: A small but eclectic chapter — Rare's pirate-trading epic, two Western-designed RPGs adapted for Japan, and a British space-trading legend that, remarkably, only ever reached Europe.
games: A real-time economic and exploration sim wrapping trading, naval combat, and swordfights around Caribbean piracy — developed by Rare and published by Ultra Games.
An obscure Metroidvania-adjacent horror-mansion adventure with real-time day/night mechanics — no European release has been found for it.
A console adaptation of Richard Garriott's PC RPG landmark, localized and published by FCI for North America — never released in Europe on NES.
Faria: A World of Mystery & Danger!
An action-RPG blending Zelda-style combat with a genuine leveling and magic system — no European release has been found for it.
A landmark British space-trading sim, ported to NES exclusively for Europe — it never received a North American or Japanese cartridge release at all.
Released in Japan as Dragon Slayer IV: Drasle Family, letting a whole family of playable characters explore one enormous connected dungeon — no European release has been found for it.
Wizardry: Proving Grounds of the Mad Overlord
A dungeon-crawler port of Sir-Tech's PC original, actually built by the Japanese studio Game Studio rather than Sir-Tech itself — never released in Europe.

title: Licensed, Movie & TV Tie-ins
blurb: Capcom and Sunsoft's Disney and superhero tie-ins remain some of the best-regarded licensed games of the whole 8-bit era.
games: A cooperative platformer built around throwing crates and enemies at each other, released in Europe about a year and a half after North America.
A darker, gadget-driven cousin to Capcom's DuckTales games, released in Europe roughly a year and a half after its North American debut.
Released in Japan simply as Batman, this Tim Burton film tie-in is still remembered as one of the best-scored and best-designed licensed games on the console.
Famous for its pogo-cane bounce mechanic and a NES soundtrack still remixed and covered decades later.
A sequel released right at the tail end of the NES's commercial life, day-and-date across all three major regions.
A licensed platformer letting Ariel alternate between swimming and on-land sections, one of Capcom's less-discussed Disney tie-ins.
A Buster Bunny-led platformer built around swappable partner characters with unique abilities.
A genuinely well-regarded platformer tie-in to the film sequel, released in Europe the year after its North American debut.
A beat-em-up developed in Japan but, unusually, never actually released there — it reached North America only, following the same pattern as its Genesis counterpart.

title: Cult Classics & Deep Cuts
blurb: The deepest cuts in the collection, including Kid Icarus's oddly reversed rollout order and Gimmick!, one of the rarest and most sought-after carts ever made.
games: A licensed platformer tied to the 1989 animated film, built around capturing and riding enemy creatures — released in Europe by Nintendo about a year after North America.

Released in Japan as Wanpaku Kokkun no Gourmet World, this cartoonish kitchen-themed platformer's European release didn't land until 1994 — around two years later, one of the last PAL NES releases at all.
Gargoyle's Quest II: The Demon Darkness
A side-scrolling spin-off starring Ghosts 'n Goblins' gargoyle antihero Firebrand, blending platforming with light RPG progression.
An unusual case of Europe getting the game first — its February 1987 European release actually preceded North America's by about five months.
Sunsoft of America rejected it outright, so it never reached North America at all — Europe only saw it as a 1993 Scandinavia-exclusive release, now one of the most expensive NES carts in existence.
A genre hybrid alternating top-down shoot-em-up corridors with an open, Zelda-style overworld to explore.
An offbeat, humor-heavy action-adventure with a surprisingly open structure for 1989 — no European release has been found for it.
A licensed conversion of Jaleco's own arcade side-scroller, actually built by the separate studio Aicom — no European release has been found for it.

Originally designed as a licensed Terminator game before the film license fell through mid-development — the Japanese and European box art kept the redesigned, fully-armored protagonist while North America's cover showed an exposed face.

title: Graphic Adventure & Horror
blurb: A genre nobody associates with the NES today, imported almost entirely by Kemco from ICOM Simulations' Mac and PC point-and-click originals.
games: A grim, item-puzzle-driven castle adventure ported from ICOM Simulations' Macintosh original, reaching Europe roughly two years after its North American debut.
Déjà Vu: A Nightmare Comes True!!
A hard-boiled noir mystery-adventure, the second of ICOM's MacVenture trilogy to reach NES — Europe's release followed about two years later.
A haunted-house horror adventure rounding out the MacVenture trilogy on NES — no European release has been found for it.
Nintendo of America's content policy stripped profanity, violence, and innuendo from this port — a hamster-in-the-microwave gag survived by oversight until roughly 250,000 carts had already shipped.
A horror-camp survival game built loosely around the slasher franchise, released exclusively in North America — no European or Japanese release ever happened.

A surreal action-platformer developed in Japan but never actually released there — its own Japanese version was cancelled, surviving only as an unreleased prototype, making the North American cart its sole official release.

title: Multiplayer, Novelty & Peripheral Games
blurb: Zapper light-gun classics, a Metal Gear sequel made without Hideo Kojima, and Bomberman's own oddly reversed regional rollout close out the collection.
games: A Zapper light-gun classic bundled with early consoles worldwide, though Europe didn't see it until roughly two years after Japan.
A launch-window title built specifically to showcase the R.O.B. robot peripheral, largely forgotten once R.O.B. itself was discontinued.
Released in Japan as the noticeably easier Mad City — the Western version raised enemy aggression, cut ammo, narrowed the roads, and trimmed four possible endings down to one.
A Metal Gear sequel made without any involvement from series creator Hideo Kojima, released only in North America and Europe.
Famously delayed in Europe by roughly two years past its North American release — long enough that many European players met the series through this game's own sequel first.
A conversion of Hudson's own 1985 Japanese original, delayed nearly four years for its North American release — no European NES cartridge release has been confirmed.
Released in Europe as Dynablaster, this sequel actually reached Japan and Europe well before its heavily delayed North American release — a reversal of the usual pattern.
An arcade fire-breathing-strongman platformer co-developed with programming studio SAS Sakata — no European NES release has been found for it.
A Looney Tunes-licensed platformer that reached Japan, North America, and Europe all within the same year, an unusually tight window for a licensed title of its era.
